podcast.title: Confrontation with Biker Gang (Early 1974)
podcast.body: By early 1974, the band's behavior was completely out of control. During a gig in Wayne, Michigan, a biker gang called the Scorpions heckled Iggy Pop for his skimpy, skin-tight leopard costume. Iggy confronted them, resulting in eggs and bottles being thrown at the stage. "By early 1974, things had really gotten out of control."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Most Dangerous Artists in Rock

podcast.title: Backstage Rider – Entertainment Requests (Bob Hope/Dwarves)
podcast.body: The rider includes bizarre entertainment requests such as "Someone dressed as Bob Hope doing fantastic Bob Hope impersonations" or, alternatively, "Seven dwarves dressed up as those dwarves out of that marvelous Walt Disney film about the woman who goes to sleep for 100 years after biting a poise and dwarf" (conflating Sleeping Beauty and Snow White, later implying Cinderella). It notes that "Tollia people are acceptable, of course. It's attitude more than height that's important here. And don't forget the pointy hats." "Or I guess this is in lieu of a Bob Hope impersonator. Seven dwarves dressed up as those dwarves out of that marvelous Walt Disney film about the woman who goes to sleep for 100 years after biting a poise and dwarf."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Backstage Rider – Guitarist's Counting Skills
podcast.body: The rider humorously highlights guitarist Chris's counting abilities, stating he "will personally count on arrival" the "six knobs" on each amplifier and describing him as "the closest thing that we have in our touring party to a mathematical genius." "Chris will personally count on arrival and trust me, he's a very good counter."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Backstage Rider – Humorous and Detailed Amp Specifications
podcast.body: The band's rider contains extremely detailed, yet humorously exaggerated, specifications for their amplifiers. For bass, it requests three Marshall VBA bass amplifiers, emphasizing their quality ("Please make sure they're good ones"). For guitar, it asks for three JCM 800 single channel master volume Marshall Amp Heads (100 watt, model 2203), requiring recent testing (within "living memory, preferably that of a goldfish"). It specifies "six knobs" (War, Pestilence, Famine, later corrected to Presence, Bass, Middle, Treble, Pre, and Post-Game) and two inputs (high and low impedance), explicitly forbidding dual-channel reverb heads or foot switches. "No, I mean recently within a living memory, preferably that of a goldfish."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Backstage Rider – Specific Catering Demands
podcast.body: Catering requirements include dinner for Iggy and two others, available at the venue or a local restaurant, with local cuisine or steak/chicken (or humorously, "endangered species, including moths and anything really cute, snake whale or nurse shark"). It explicitly states that "Cauliflower and broccoli cut into individual florets and then thrown immediately in the garbage." For loadout, two enormous pizzas are requested, often left on the bus to be discarded later due to their unwieldy size. "Cauliflower and broccoli cut into individual florets and then thrown immediately in the garbage."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Band Breakup and Legendary Status
podcast.body: The proposed rematch with the Scorpions never happened, as The Stooges broke up shortly after the incident. This true story cemented their legend as "America's most dangerous rock and roll band." "That never happened, blessedly, because the Stooges then broke up."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Most Dangerous Artists in Rock

podcast.title: Extreme Behavior and Drug Use
podcast.body: The Stooges were known for their wild and intense performances, with Iggy Pop being particularly unhinged. The band extensively used drugs, including heroin and Angel Dust, leading to self-destructive behavior and an out-of-control reputation. "They were on every drug known to man all the way up to heroin and Angel Dust."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Most Dangerous Artists in Rock

podcast.title: Iggy Pop's Beating and Challenge
podcast.body: While the rest of the band fled, Iggy Pop remained to confront the bikers, jumping into the crowd and receiving a severe beating before being dragged out, possibly saving his life. Days later, Iggy appeared on the radio, promoting an upcoming show and boldly challenging the Scorpions to a rematch. "He stayed there to confront the bikers, jumping into the crowd. And he got a pretty good beating."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Most Dangerous Artists in Rock

podcast.title: Iggy Pop's Stage Antics
podcast.body: Iggy Pop was notorious for scaring audiences with his antics, which included smearing peanut butter on himself and carving his body with broken glass from bottles thrown at him on stage. "He'd smear peanut butter all over himself and often carve himself up with broken glass from the beer bottles that were thrown at him on stage."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Most Dangerous Artists in Rock

podcast.title: Implied Soviet Blacklist - Violence
podcast.body: Though listed as "The Stages" on the USSR's 1985 "not recommended music" list, it is speculated that Soviet authorities were likely referring to Iggy Pop and The Stooges when they cited "Violence" as a reason for prohibition. This indicates the perceived aggressive or disruptive influence of their music. "The Stages, I think they meant Iggy Pop and the Stooges, Violence, ACDC, Neo-Fascism and Violence."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Most Important Post-Garage Rock Band
podcast.body: Iggy Pop and the Stooges were retrospectively identified as the most important of the post-Garage Rock bands. Known for being "drugged out, whacked out, and totally crazy," they were one of the few groups that continued to appeal to audiences after the original Garage Rock sound was thought to be "done" by the late 1960s, and they served as a key inspiration for the first Garage Rock revival (punk). "But in retrospect, the most important of the post garage rock bands, was Iggy Pop and the Stooges."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alt Rock Revivals Part 4: Garage Rock

podcast.title: Motor City Ancestor
podcast.body: Iggy Pop and the Stooges are cited as "Motor City ancestors" who influenced the Detroit and Michigan underground indie scene, especially inspiring bands like The White Stripes and Yeah Yeah Yeahs. "From there, they ingratiated themselves into the Detroit and Michigan underground indie scene, all of whom had something in common with motor city ancestors like the Stooges and the MC5."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Elton John Gorilla Suit Incident – Richards, Atlanta, October 1973
xref.body: In October 1973, Iggy Pop and the Stooges were playing at Richards in Atlanta at the same time Elton John was touring America. Elton — engaged in a semi-friendly rivalry with David Bowie, who was a known Stooges supporter — decided to crash the show dressed in a full gorilla suit to surprise Iggy on stage. A photographer from Detroit music magazine *Creem* was tipped off. No one warned Iggy that this was planned, and no one warned Elton that Iggy was heavily intoxicated on speed that night. When Elton bounded onto the stage in the gorilla suit, Iggy genuinely believed it was a real gorilla, was terrified, and fled the stage. The incident was captured on film. After Elton removed the gorilla head and multiple people calmed Iggy down, the show resumed and the two performed several songs together — Iggy bare-chested, Elton still in the suit. "Iggy thought it was an actual gorilla. And this freak out is captured on film."

xref.title: Reunion at Coachella Festival (2003)
xref.body: The surviving members of Iggy Pop and the Stooges officially reunited for a performance at the Coachella Festival on April 27, 2003. "And so it came to pass that Iggy Pop and the Stooges, the surviving members, performed at the Coachella Festival on April 27th, 2003."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Cleveland Reception
xref.body: Music fans in Cleveland had been exposed to performances by Iggy Pop and The Stooges over the years, which made a significant impression and helped foster the development of extreme, experimental groups in the city. "music fans in Cleveland had been treated to performances by the stuages and Iggy Pop and the Velvet Underground over the years. And they had all made quite the impression."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Creation of Ziggy Stardust
xref.body: Building on glam rock concepts, Bowie developed the character Ziggy Stardust. This persona was inspired by the outrageous behavior of Iggy Pop and The Stooges, the artsy "scummy" persona of Lou Reed and the Velvet Underground, the "god-alien" self-perception of Vince Taylor, and the "space travel obsessed" persona of Norman Odom, also known as the Legendary Stardust Cowboy. Bowie combined these influences, changing "Iggy" to "Ziggy" and adopting "Stardust" as the surname. "He invented an entire character completely rooted in glam rock concepts that borrowed from the outrageous behavior of another new friend, Iggy Pop... So Bowie, taking all this information, changed Iggy to Ziggy and adopted Stardust as a surname and thus Ziggy Stardust was born."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Surprising History of Glam Rock

xref.title: Drug Use and Mental Instability
xref.body: Around the same time Jonathan Richmond was recording "Roadrunner" (circa 1971), Iggy Pop and The Stooges were dropped from their record label and were increasingly involved with hard drugs. Iggy was known for being in an almost constant state of mental instability, characterized by crazy, animalistic, demonic, and self-destructive stage antics. "They were also getting deeper into hard, hard drugs."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Failed Attempt to Sign The Stooges
xref.body: Despite his dramatic stage appearance in a gorilla suit, Elton John's mutual admiration with Iggy Pop and The Stooges did not result in him signing the band to a record contract. "Elton never did sign him or the band to a record contract."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Featured in Punk Magazine
xref.body: The fanzine "Punk," which appeared at the end of 1975, covered Iggy Pop and The Stooges, among other raw, primitive garage bands from the 60s and artists in the burgeoning CBGB scene. "It also covered Iggy Pop and the Stooges, The New York Dolls, and even some of their raw, primitive garage bands from the 60s like Question Mark and Mysterians."

xref.title: Influence on "Punk" Terminology
xref.body: Lester Banks, a Detroit rock writer, wrote extensively about the kind of rock played by Iggy Pop and The Stooges, among other similar artists, contributing to the initial discourse around this raw sound. Later, Legs McNeill, a significant fan and founder of the "Punk" fanzine, included Iggy Pop among the artists he admired and wrote about, cementing his status within the burgeoning punk scene. "Lester Banks began spewing out thousands and thousands of rapturous words on the kind of rock played by the Count Five, Iggy Pop and the Stooges and others of their ilk."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Influence on "Punk" Terminology
xref.body: Lester Banks, a Detroit rock writer, extensively covered the kind of rock performed by The Stooges and Iggy Pop. His writings helped to shape the early critical understanding of this raw and energetic style of music, which was later associated with the "punk" aesthetic. "Lester Banks began spewing out thousands and thousands of rapturous words on the kind of rock played by the Count Five, Iggy Pop and the Stooges and others of their ilk."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Influence on Punk Rock
xref.body: Despite Bowie's patronage, Iggy Pop and The Stooges remained fringe characters, a status embraced by their particular fanbase. The band's first three albums, influenced by Bowie's acceptance of their "weirdness," became some of the most important templates for the genre that would eventually be called punk rock. "And this is how the first three Stooges albums became some of the most important templates for what would be eventually called punk rock."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Influenced Major Artists
xref.body: The Velvet Underground is credited with awakening and influencing a wide array of prominent artists and bands, including David Bowie, Roxy Music, The Doors, Patti Smith, Iggy Pop and the Stooges, U2, Joy Division, The Pixies, The Sex Pistols, Talking Heads, The Cure, Kraftwerk, R.E.M., Simple Minds, The Strokes, and The Psychedelic Furs, whose name derived from a Velvet Underground song. "Here is a list of just some of the few who claimed to have been awakened by the velvet underground and then incorporated some of whatever they were doing into their music."

xref.title: Nihilistic Parallel with The Stooges
xref.body: The Velvet Underground are noted for being as nihilistic as Iggy Pop and The Stooges, establishing a parallel in their challenging and dark artistic approach. "They were every bit as nihilistic as the Velvet Underground and violent to boot."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About Iggy Pop

xref.title: Patronage of Iggy Pop and The Stooges
xref.body: Bowie was a great admirer and musical hero of Iggy Pop, fascinated by his craziness, almost constant mental instability, and ability to see beyond the drugs and self-destructive stage antics to Iggy's intelligence. Bowie convinced his manager to take on Iggy and The Stooges as a project, providing a cash injection that funded their *Raw Power* album. He later visited Iggy when he was in a mental hospital. Bowie's acceptance of Iggy also helped propel the first three Stooges albums to become important templates for punk rock. "Iggy's craziness had made him into one of Bowie's musical heroes."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Pioneers of Punk and Alternative Rock
xref.body: Iggy Pop and the Stooges were "absolutely bloody essential" in laying the groundwork for all the punk, alternative, and New Rock music that emerged in subsequent decades, suggesting that the landscape of music would be vastly different without their influence. "Iggy Pop and the Stooges were absolutely bloody essential in setting the stage for all the punk, alternative, and New Rock that was to come in the decades ahead."
